An Ontology-Based Genus Identification and Decision-Support Model for Paleocene–Eocene Benthic Foraminifera
KÜBRA YAYAN1
1Department of Geological Engineering, Faculty of Engineering and Architecture, Eskişehir Osmangazi University, 26480 Eskişehir, Türkiye
Corresponding author: Kübra Yayan (e-mail: kokur@ogu.edu.tr).

This work was carried out within the benthic foraminiferal taxonomy and numerical identification research line of the Department of Geological Engineering, Eskişehir Osmangazi University, without external funding.

ABSTRACT Genus-level identification of Paleocene–Eocene benthic foraminifera in thin section relies on expert morphological interpretation that is difficult to reproduce. This study presents an ontology-based decision-support model that encodes this expertise as an auditable knowledge base: 21 controlled morphological characters with 108 states and 75 genera in three wall-composition modules, described by 706 rule cards graded into mandatory, diagnostic, supporting, and contradictory evidence. The knowledge base is published as an OWL 2 ontology with cardinality and disjointness axioms, verified with HermiT, and as a property graph. A deterministic engine treats unobservable characters as neutral rather than absent and returns a ranked list of genera with one of five graded confidence states; a decision-tree walk and a World Register of Marine Species check complete the workflow. After an automated integrity audit and repair, the engine ranks the leaf genus first on 53 of 104 decision paths, and 17 of its 29 CONFIRMED_GENUS outputs are correct, compared with 14 of 48 before repair. In a Monte Carlo simulation on rule-derived profiles with about 30% of the characters masked and 5% state noise, the graded engine reaches 43.7% top-1 and 61.0% top-3 agreement, against 7.3% and 21.2% for a classical eliminative multi-access key, and its rankings remain stable under alternative weightings (rank-biased overlap 0.93–0.99). A zero-shot stress test of a general-purpose vision-language model on 150 published image panels yields 3.2% top-1 agreement with overconfident states, showing that such models can draft observations for expert review but cannot replace the expert-supervised ontology layer.

INTRODUCTION

Foraminifera are predominantly marine unicellular eukaryotes whose tests may be organic, agglutinated from sediment particles, or secreted as calcium carbonate with a porcelaneous or hyaline wall [1]. Their readily preserved tests make them one of the main tools of biostratigraphy, relative dating, paleoenvironmental interpretation, and paleobathymetry [2], [3]. Paleocene–Eocene benthic assemblages, and larger benthic foraminifera (LBF) in particular, have been described in detail from many regions of Türkiye (Van, Ordu, Ankara–Polatlı, Malatya, Aksaray, Kayseri, Sivas, and others), introducing numerous new genera and species [4]–[22].

Several of the taxa treated in this literature are encoded as genus nodes in the present ontology, among them Ranikothalia [6], Laffitteina [13], Pseudolacazina [11], [15], Alveolina [17], Fabularia and Kathina [18], Cuvillierina [19], Miscellanea [22], Ornatorotalia and Granorotalia [5], and Orbitoclypeus and Discocyclina [21]. Other genera from the same body of work, including Karsella [12], Orduina [8], Malatyna [10], [14], Vania [16], and Haymanella, Kayseriella, Elazigella, and Orduella [9], informed the design of the character vocabulary but are not yet encoded as genus nodes; their inclusion is planned for the next release (Section X).

Despite this knowledge, genus-level identification in thin section still depends largely on the experience of a specialist and is slowed and made subjective by inconsistent terminology, critical characters hidden by section orientation or preservation, and limited reproducibility between specialists. Deep-learning image classifiers have accelerated identification [23]–[25] but generally act as black boxes: they do not state the morphological evidence of a decision, their class set is fixed by the training data, and they do not map onto the dichotomous keys of the paleontological literature [26].

This study proposes an ontology-based decision-support model whose primary contribution is the knowledge model and its deterministic inference, not image recognition. It covers agglutinated, porcelaneous, and hyaline genera and is built on 21 controlled morphological characters (CHR_01–CHR_21), designed from the original descriptions of seven pilot taxa, Karsella hottingeri [12], Pseudolacazina oeztemueri [15], Alveolina haymanaensis [17], Discocyclina seunesi [21], Laffitteina erki [13], Orbitoclypeus haymanaensis [21], and Ranikothalia sindensis [6], and extended to 75 genera by literature synthesis. The system narrows the candidate set, shows the character matches and the evidence behind each result, and leaves the taxonomic decision to the specialist.

The contributions of this article are: (1) a formal genus-level identification ontology for Paleocene–Eocene benthic foraminifera with OWL 2 cardinality and disjointness axioms; (2) a deterministic inference framework that maps an observation set, through 706 rule cards graded by evidence level, onto one of five confidence states, formalized in equations and pseudocode; (3) an evaluation logic that never equates unobservable characters with absence; (4) linkage of the output to taxonomic validity (WoRMS) and paleoenvironmental records; (5) an open-access Web implementation on a graph database with a scripted integrity audit and repair; and (6) a reproducible evaluation comprising an internal consistency test, a Monte Carlo comparison with an eliminative multi-access key, counterfactual ablations, a weight and threshold sensitivity analysis, and a zero-shot vision-language-model stress test.

Section II reviews related work, Section III the model design, Section IV the ontology and knowledge base, Section V the decision-tree walk, Section VI the scoring engine, and Section VII the optional image layer; Section VIII reports the evaluation, Section IX discusses limitations, and Section X concludes.
RELATED WORK

Four lines of work bear on accelerating foraminiferal identification: deep-learning image classification, ontology- and rule-based taxonomic expert systems, interactive multi-access identification keys, and general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) applied to scientific images; this section reviews each and positions the proposed model.
A. DEEP-LEARNING-BASED FORAMINIFERAL CLASSIFICATION

Hsiang et al. assembled the Endless Forams data set of more than 34,000 images of planktonic foraminifera and reached near-expert accuracy with a VGG architecture [23]; Mitra et al. compared convolutional neural network (CNN) identification of planktic species with human performance [24], and Marchant et al. built a CNN workflow that counts and classifies foraminifera in sediment cores [25]. Earlier work by the author and colleagues addressed CNN classification [27] and multi-label identification [28] of benthic foraminifera. Post-hoc explanations such as Grad-CAM [29] highlight image regions but name no morphological character, so inherently interpretable models are preferable for high-stakes decisions [26]. These studies achieve high accuracy, but they state no morphological evidence, fix the class set by the training data, and do not follow the step-wise logic of classical keys.
B. ONTOLOGY- AND RULE-BASED TAXONOMIC EXPERT SYSTEMS

Rule-based taxonomic expert systems are not new: Heymans et al. separated Opuntia (Cactaceae) species from family to species level with a CLIPS rule base [30], and Gerber et al. modeled Afrotropical bee taxonomy as a description-logic ontology with automated reasoning in a Web application [31]. Phenotype ontologies such as PATO (entity–quality pairs) and the OBO Foundry principles offer reusable patterns for morphological characters [32]–[34]. Such systems are transparent, but character entry is manual and the rules are usually binary, without evidence-weighted scoring or multi-level confidence states.
C. INTERACTIVE AND MULTI-ACCESS IDENTIFICATION KEYS

The closest functional predecessors of the proposed model are multi-access (free-access) identification keys. DELTA introduced a general format for coding taxonomic descriptions as character matrices from which conventional and interactive keys (Intkey) are generated [35]; Lucid [36] and Xper2/Xper3 [37], [38] let the user enter any available character in any order and discard taxa incompatible with the entered states. Such keys already cope with characters missing from a specimen and are widely used in biodiversity informatics.

The proposed model differs from these tools in five respects. First, each genus–character statement carries one of four evidence levels with distinct roles (mandatory statements gate the candidate set, diagnostic ones discriminate, supporting ones add weak evidence, contradictory ones penalize), whereas classical keys treat all characters as equally eliminatory, optionally with a mismatch tolerance. Second, NOT_OBSERVABLE (region not visible) is separated from ABSENT (region visible, feature missing) and UNCERTAIN, which is critical for orientation-dependent characters. Third, the output is one of five graded confidence states rather than a residual list of taxa. Fourth, the genus is checked against its accepted name in WoRMS [39]. Fifth, the knowledge base is an OWL 2 ontology [40] and a queryable property graph rather than a closed matrix format.
D. VISION-LANGUAGE MODELS IN SCIENTIFIC IMAGE ANALYSIS

General-purpose VLMs have recently been evaluated on scientific images: the VLM4Bio benchmark of Maruf et al. found substantial inconsistency and a risk of hallucination when 12 VLMs extracted fine-grained traits from fish, bird, and butterfly images [41], and Verma et al. judged the reliability of large VLMs on microscopy images limited without domain-specific grounding [42]. VLM output should therefore be confined to a structured, auditable intermediate step rather than used as a taxonomic decision.
E. POSITIONING OF THE PRESENT WORK

Table I compares the proposed model with these approaches. Its main contribution is the explicit knowledge model and the deterministic inference over it: a controlled character ontology, graded rule cards, and a scoring engine whose every decision can be traced to morphological statements; the optional VLM layer only drafts an observation sheet in the same vocabulary, which the specialist reviews and the engine evaluates like manual input. To the author’s knowledge, this combination has not previously been implemented for Paleocene–Eocene benthic foraminifera.

MODEL DESIGN AND KNOWLEDGE LAYERS

The model consists of four stacked knowledge layers. The character model defines the features observable in thin section through a controlled vocabulary, removing terminological ambiguity. The rule base defines each genus by these characters and grades every criterion by evidence level. The inference layer uses this knowledge in two forms: a step-wise decision-tree walk corresponding to classical identification keys and a scoring engine that evaluates all available observations at once. The context layer links the resulting genus to its current taxonomic validity and known paleoenvironmental preference. The layers follow the paleontologist’s workflow: describe what is seen, test which genera it fits, and place the result in its taxonomic and environmental context.

Fig. 1 shows how the layers are connected: observations entered by the user, or drafted by the optional image pre-extraction layer and reviewed by the user, are converted into the 21 controlled characters, which feed both inference paths over one rule base. The scoring engine returns a ranked list of genera with one of five confidence states; the decision-tree walk returns the leaf genus or, after a “Not observable” answer, the genera that remain reachable (Section V). Both results are linked to taxonomic validity and paleoenvironmental context.
A. TWO MODES OF THE IDENTIFICATION PROCESS

The step-wise interrogation imitates a classical identification key, asking one morphological question per stage, and is fast for well-preserved sections; the direct entry of every visible character, in any order, evaluates all genera of the module at once and suits oblique or partial sections. The genus reached is checked against the current taxonomic register and, where available, shown with paleoenvironmental information; if the register cannot be reached, identification continues without this context.

ONTOLOGY AND CHARACTER MODEL

The core of the ontology is a single observation pattern in which every morphological character has a unique identifier: Specimen → Character ID → Observed Value → Observation State. The observation state is PRESENT (clearly observable), ABSENT (clearly missing in a section in which it should be visible), NOT_OBSERVABLE (not evaluable because of section orientation, preservation, or image quality; not equivalent to ABSENT), or UNCERTAIN (visible but not determinable with confidence); this distinction underlies the neutral-evidence mechanism of the scoring engine (Section VI).

The 21 characters form four functional groups (Table II): Core (wall composition, test shape, and chamber organization), Internal Architecture (internal structure, embryonic apparatus, and chamberlets), Additional Diagnostic (e.g., aperture, marginal cord, and dimorphism), and Section (CHR_21, which records section orientation as context for the other observations and is not itself scored; see Section VI-A). The vocabulary has 108 substantive character states; with 40 response tokens (NOT_OBSERVABLE and UNCERTAIN for CHR_02–CHR_20, UNCERTAIN only for the entry character CHR_01, and UNKNOWN for CHR_21) it contains 148 coded values, shared by the three composition modules.

At genus level the ontology covers 75 genera, 25 in each module (Table III); because wall composition (CHR_01) is the entry character, answering it reduces the candidate set from 75 to 25 genera. Each genus is defined by rule cards graded by evidence level, each linked to one or more characters and their expected states, so that a free-text description becomes a set of individually testable statements. The ontology is stored as an OWL 2 file for reuse and queried at run time through a property graph in which the relations among characters, genera, and rules can be traced directly (Sections IV-B and IV-C).

The genera were selected because they (i) are recorded from Paleocene–Eocene Tethyan shallow-marine or associated assemblages in the reference classifications [1], [2] or the Turkish literature [4]–[22], (ii) can be recognized in thin section with the vocabulary of Table II, and (iii) are frequent in routine biostratigraphic work or commonly confused with such genera. The equal module size is a design choice, not a statement about diversity, and the list is not exhaustive: common Tethyan Eocene genera such as Orbitolites, Opertorbitolites, Asterigerina, Fabiania, Halkyardia, and Sphaerogypsina will be added with the Turkish genera of Section I. Agglutinated genera more often identified from washed deep-water residues (e.g., Rhabdammina, Rhizammina, Bathysiphon, Caudammina, Rzehakina, Karrerulina) are retained because they occur in thin sections of hemipelagic and deep-shelf intervals at Paleogene platform margins and must be separated from shallow-water tubular and coiled forms.

The 75 genera are encoded by 706 rule items (Table IV): 460 (65.2%) are mapped to at least one character–state pair and can contribute to a score, 14 reference a character without a state, and 232 express compound situations not reducible to one pair (e.g., “wall conspicuously constructed from relatively coarse sediment grains”); the 246 rules without a pair are shown as observation hints with zero score (Section VI). The 500 rule-to-character mappings carry a mapping confidence (HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW for 365, 108, and 27). As CONFIRMED_GENUS requires a matched diagnostic rule (Section VI-C), a genus without a scoring diagnostic rule can reach at most PROBABLE_GENUS; after the repair of Section IV-B this applies to 28 genera whose diagnostic statements rely on qualifiers not yet in the vocabulary (e.g., branching, surface ornament, canal systems, chamber proportions). These statements are kept as hints rather than mapped to a generic proxy state, and extending the vocabulary for them is the first target of the next rule-card revision.

A. KNOWLEDGE ACQUISITION PROTOCOL
The rule cards were built with the following protocol, which is also the procedure to be followed when the ontology is extended.

Source selection: For every genus, the original description and the most recent emended diagnosis were collected, supplemented by the reference classifications of Loeblich and Tappan [1] and BouDagher-Fadel [2] and by the Turkish Paleocene–Eocene literature [4]–[22]. Sources had to provide a genus-level diagnosis and thin-section illustrations; the terminology was normalized against [43].
Statement extraction: Each diagnosis was split into atomic morphological statements, each concerning a single structure (e.g., “secondary chamberlets absent”).

Terminological normalization: Each statement was mapped onto the controlled vocabulary with the illustrated glossary of Hottinger [43] as reference. Synonyms are merged (e.g., “alveoles” and “secondary chamberlets” both map to CHR_11), whereas different structures are kept apart even when often confused (e.g., STREPTOSPIRAL and GLOMOSPIRAL in CHR_06, or serial arrangement in CHR_05 versus coiling in CHR_06).
Evidence-level assignment: Each statement was assigned an evidence level according to the criteria in Table V.

Character–state mapping: Each rule was mapped to one or more character–state pairs with a mapping confidence; statements that cannot be reduced to such pairs were retained as observation hints.

Conflict resolution: Where sources disagree, the most recent emended diagnosis is followed and the genus concept accepted in WoRMS [39] is used; statements that remain disputed are downgraded to supporting level or recorded as notes, and genera whose placement is disputed are flagged (e.g., Barattolites).

The character and rule sets originate from the seven pilot taxa and were extended to the 75 genera by literature synthesis; their internal consistency is controlled by the integrity audit and logged repair of Section IV-B, which are rerun before every release.
B. ONTOLOGY ENGINEERING AND QUALITY EVALUATION

Methodology: Development followed METHONTOLOGY [44] with the requirements specification of NeOn [45]: (i) specification of scope and competency questions (CQs) [46]; (ii) conceptualization of characters, states, genera, rules, and decision questions from the reference document of the project; (iii) formalization of the vocabulary and rule structure; (iv) implementation as a JSON master data set from which the OWL 2 file and the property graph are generated; and (v) evaluation by reasoning, CQ answering, and a knowledge-base integrity audit.

Knowledge-base integrity audit and repair: OWL consistency does not guarantee that the rule cards are free of domain errors, so an automated audit (eval/audit.py) checks for: (a) contradictory rules equal to a positive rule of the same genus; (b) mandatory rules conflicting with another mandatory or diagnostic rule on the same character; (c) negated rule texts with positive mappings (polarity screen); (d) character–state pairs counted more than once within a genus, directly or through implication (by two diagnostic or supporting rules, or by a mandatory and a diagnostic rule); (e) unmapped mandatory rules; (f) genera without a scoring diagnostic rule; (g) tree answers outside the controlled vocabulary; (h) characters queried again along one path; and (i) genera not assigned to exactly one module. Two logged scripts that operate only on rule texts and trees, never on evaluation outcomes, repaired the findings (eval/apply_audit_fixes.py, 67 mapping edits; eval/bind_tree_vocabulary.py, 7 answer bindings): each rule is re-mapped to the state its text states or, where the vocabulary cannot express a qualifier (e.g., “low trochospiral” or “Lacazina-type pillar pattern absent”), returned to a non-scoring hint instead of a misleading proxy; five off-vocabulary tree answers were bound to controlled states (e.g., “flattened/sigmoid serial organization” to the state used for the same concept in the rule card of Rzehakina), and two complement answers became routing answers resolved by the next character-bound question. Across the nine categories, the audit counts changed from 17, 10, 4, 25, 27, 18, 7, 11, and 0 to 0, 0, 3, 0, 28, 28, 0, 11, and 0. The three remaining polarity flags are not inverted mappings on inspection; the additional unmapped mandatory rule (Pseudolacazina M4, “partitions and/or pillars”) is a disjunction across two characters that the evaluator does not support; and the increase in (f) reflects removed diagnostic mappings that only repeated a mandatory pair or misrepresented the text. Three of the 18 genera originally lacking a scoring diagnostic rule received a literal mapping (Hauerina; Orbitoclypeus and Nemkovella, via the embryonic-apparatus state of the corresponding tree answer). The repaired master files, every edit with its textual basis, and the item-by-item audit listings before and after repair are given in Supplementary Material S9.
C. GRAPH DATABASE LAYER

At run time the knowledge base is held in a Neo4j v5 property graph [51] that mirrors the OWL schema (Fig. 2), with node labels Module, Genus, Character, Value, RuleItem, Question, Outcome, ObservationState, Status, and TaxonProfile and relationship types BELONGS_TO, HAS_RULE (with the evidence level), REFERS_TO (with expected state and mapping confidence), ALLOWS, CLOSEST_COMPARISON, TREE_ENTRY, ASKS_ABOUT, ANSWER, and HAS_REFERENCE_SPECIES/HAS_ENVIRONMENT_PROFILE. TaxonProfile nodes, which hold the paleoenvironmental records described below, and WormsCache nodes are operational data without an OWL counterpart. Eleven uniqueness constraints guard the identifiers. Graph and OWL file are generated from the same JSON master files, so they cannot drift apart, and the import script verifies the expected node counts. WoRMS responses are cached (WormsCache) for seven days with a 3-s timeout, so identification does not depend on the external service.

In the application, the Taxon Environment Records section of the Geological Context page presents 18 paleoenvironmental records (seven at species and eleven at genus level) compiled from the project literature, with depth, habitat, and source displayed in English. Six of them are linked to genera of the identification ontology; for the other twelve (e.g., Karsella hottingeri, Orbitolites, and Opertorbitolites) the system states explicitly that the record is “Not yet linked to diagnostic ontology,” so that the gap is reported rather than hidden. Species-level records are not automatically generalized to the entire genus.
D. RELATION TO EXISTING PHENOTYPE ONTOLOGIES

The observation pattern corresponds to the entity–quality pattern of phenotype ontologies: a character such as CHR_17 (marginal cord) is an anatomical entity and its states (PRESENT, WEAK, STRONG) are qualities [32], [33]. As the OBO Foundry has no foraminiferal anatomy ontology [34] and unicellular tests do not map onto metazoan anatomy, the characters are defined locally, annotated with their definition and page in the Hottinger glossary [43] (skos:definition [52], dcterms:source [53]); qualities with a general counterpart (e.g., presence, absence, relative size) will be linked to PATO with skos:closeMatch in the next release.
E. STRATIGRAPHIC SCOPE AND GEOLOGICAL CONTEXT

The ontology targets the Paleocene–Eocene, chiefly the Thanetian–Priabonian (≈59.2–33.9 Ma; SBZ 3–20, with the regional Ilerdian–Cuisian equivalent to the Ypresian) [2], [54]–[56]. Middle–Late Eocene genera (e.g., Lacazinella, Spiroclypeus) and the Turkish Lutetian–Priabonian literature [7], [14], [20] are in scope; the Danian–Selandian (SBZ 1–2) is covered only through genera ranging into it.

The genus list also contains long-ranging smaller benthic genera (e.g., Ammodiscus, Quinqueloculina, and Lenticulina) that are not restricted to the Paleocene–Eocene but must be separated from the larger forms in practice. Zone equivalents follow [55], [56]; absolute ages are approximate. Geological age is not an identification criterion: stratigraphic information is shown only as context, and, once curated (the corresponding field of Supplementary Material S1 is not yet complete), the stratigraphic range of each genus will only be used to warn the user when an identification is inconsistent with the stated age of the sample.
DECISION-TREE WALK

Each composition module has its own question–answer tree, transcribed from the identification key of the project’s reference document (Paleocene–Eocene Benthic Foraminifera Genus Identification Ontology v1.0; Supplementary Material S3 provides the OWL file and the three JSON trees but not this document). Question nodes refer to morphological characters where possible and answers to their states; leaves are genera or explicit outcomes (INDETERMINATE or a redirection to another branch). The walk starts with the wall-composition question, which selects the module, and follows the branch of each answer.

The trees follow four design principles: (i) they start with characters robust to section orientation (wall composition and septation); (ii) they proceed from gross architecture (test shape, chamber organization, coiling) to internal architecture (chamberlets, pillars, embryonic apparatus); (iii) orientation-dependent characters are asked as late as possible, and five such nodes carry a section-sensitivity flag that the interface can display as a warning; and (iv) where the literature keys rely on a gestalt that the vocabulary cannot express, a composite question with an observation hint is kept; 22 of the 78 nodes are of this type and are not bound to a character, which limits the agreement between the two inference paths (Section VIII-B).

Table IX summarizes the trees: 78 question nodes lead through 104 root-to-leaf paths to all 75 genera (15 genera reachable by more than one path). The deepest path needs ten questions in the porcelaneous module, where lacazinid and complex milioline genera require multi-stage interrogation of internal structure, and seven in the agglutinated module, where early questions on septation and test shape narrow the candidates quickly. Every answer of a character-bound question carries a controlled state or an explicit binding to a state of another character, or is a routing answer resolved by the next character-bound question (Section IV-B).

When the user selects “Not observable / Not sure,” the walk does not stop but returns all genera reachable from that node and the remaining branches, so that a single unobservable character does not end the identification; this is the decision-tree counterpart of the neutral-evidence mechanism of the engine. The walk assigns no confidence state: it returns the leaf genus, an explicit outcome, or the reachable set. Confidence states are produced only by the scoring engine, to which the observations of each path are passed in the consistency test of Section VIII-B.
RULE-BASED SCORING ENGINE

Whereas the decision-tree walk follows one path, the scoring engine evaluates all genera of a module in parallel against the same observation set. The definitions below correspond one-to-one to the implementation in api/src/services/scoring.js of the evaluated version, which is used by the API and the test suite; an independent Python implementation (eval/consistency_and_audit.py) reproduces its results on all decision-tree paths (Section VIII-B).
A. OBSERVATIONS AND RULE EVALUATION

Let 𝒞 be the set of 21 characters and Vc the controlled states of character c. An observation set O assigns to each character an observation state sc ∈ {PRESENT, ABSENT, NOT_OBSERVABLE, UNCERTAIN} and, where applicable, a state vc ∈ Vc; characters not entered are treated as NOT_OBSERVABLE. The observation state only decides whether c is evaluable; whether a rule holds is decided by the recorded state vc. The absence of a structure is therefore recorded as the state vc = ABSENT of an evaluable character (e.g., CHR_03, CHR_11, or CHR_17), which is why ABSENT occurs both as an observation state and as a controlled state. If CHR_01 itself is recorded as NOT_OBSERVABLE or UNCERTAIN, no module is selected and all 75 genera are evaluated. A character–state pair (c, v) holds, h(c, v) = 1, if v ∈ Hc(O); it is violated, h(c, v) = 0, if Hc(O) ≠ ∅ and v ∉ Hc(O); otherwise, when Hc(O) = ∅, it is undetermined, h(c, v) = ⊥. Implication can therefore determine a character that was not entered, so the user need not enter the same information twice, and a mapping such as CHR_09 = BISERIAL_TO_UNISERIAL, which implies two states of CHR_05, is handled without conflict.

C. CONFIDENCE STATES

The engine reports one of five confidence states (Algorithm 1). The thresholds are fixed a priori: at least τobs = 2 evaluable characters besides CHR_01 for any genus-level state and τNM = 3 for NO_MATCH_WITHIN_CORE_TAXA, so that a single observation never yields a positive or negative verdict (Section VIII-E). CHR_01 is excluded from n(O) and from the mandatory test of line 8 because every genus of the selected module matches its wall-composition rule, which would otherwise meet both safeguards. The graded report conveys the strength of the evidence; NO_MATCH_WITHIN_CORE_TAXA is a valid, informative result rather than a forced match.

Operationally, CONFIRMED_GENUS requires at least τobs evaluable characters besides CHR_01, a matched and no violated mandatory rule on another character, a matched diagnostic rule, no matched contradiction, and separation from the runner-up by at least δ = 1 point and by a diagnostic character–state pair that the runner-up does not match diagnostically (line 10). PROBABLE_GENUS marks an uncontradicted leader whose mapped diagnostic rules are not observable (line 12) or the only active genus (line 14); CANDIDATE_GENUS marks tied scores (line 11), a leader not separated from the runner-up (line 13), or a contradicted leader. INDETERMINATE results from fewer than τobs such characters, no matched mandatory rule beyond CHR_01 (line 8), or exclusion of every genus with fewer than τNM evaluable characters (line 6), and NO_MATCH_WITHIN_CORE_TAXA from exclusion of every genus with at least τNM evaluable characters (line 6).

The PROBABLE test (line 12) deliberately precedes the separation test (line 13): without a matched diagnostic rule, 𝒟(g1) is empty and sep cannot hold when a runner-up exists, so in the opposite order a leader whose diagnostic characters are merely unobservable could never be PROBABLE_GENUS. The price is that PROBABLE_GENUS may be issued with a one-point margin, e.g., from a single supporting rule; the stricter variant requiring Δ ≥ wM = 3 at line 12 is ablation A6 (Section VIII-D).
D. RATIONALE FOR THE EVIDENCE WEIGHTS

The mandatory weight (+3) is deliberately lower than the diagnostic weight (+5). Mandatory rules act mainly as an eligibility gate, whose violation excludes a genus (4), and are by construction shared by many genera of a module (e.g., agglutinated wall, multichambered test), so a high weight would reward genera merely for having many generic mandatory rules. Diagnostic rules encode the features that separate a genus from its closest comparison genera and must dominate the ranking among the genera that pass the gate. Supporting rules (+1) only break near-ties, and contradictory rules (−5) are weighted like diagnostic rules because they are diagnostic of a confusable genus; the sensitivity to these choices is quantified in Section VIII-E.
E. WORKED EXAMPLE

The discriminating role of the diagnostic rules is illustrated by Ammodiscus and Glomospira, which share the mandatory rules on agglutinated wall, undivided tubular chamber, and absence of septa (Table XI). With coiling type (CHR_06) and coiling plane (CHR_07) both observed (scenario A), Ammodiscus matches both diagnostic rules and scores 19, whereas Glomospira matches none and triggers its contradictory rule on regular planispiral coiling (score 4); the runner-up is Rhizammina (7), and Ammodiscus is reported as CONFIRMED_GENUS with Δ = 12. When the coiling plane cannot be judged in a tangential section (scenario B), D2 becomes NEUTRAL instead of counting against either genus: Ammodiscus falls to 14 and the margin to 7, but it remains CONFIRMED_GENUS because D1 still separates it. Treating unobservable characters as ABSENT (ablation A1) would instead violate a mandatory rule of every agglutinated genus in both scenarios, since unentered characters such as CHR_02 in rule M2 would count as absent, and the engine would return NO_MATCH_WITHIN_CORE_TAXA, the failure the neutral state prevents.

OPTIONAL AUXILIARY LAYER: CHARACTER PRE-EXTRACTION FROM IMAGES

So far, the observations are assumed to be entered by a specialist. To speed up data entry, an optional auxiliary layer (called Vision Observer in the software) drafts the observation sheet from a thin-section image with optional context (locality, age, optical conditions, scale, and views), proposing a value for each of the 21 characters and leaving every character it cannot interpret as NOT_OBSERVABLE. The draft is not an identification: after review by the user it enters the rule base exactly like manual input and is evaluated by the deterministic logic of Section VI. When the layer is disabled, the ontology, the decision tree, and the engine work unchanged; the taxonomic claim of the study rests on the morphological rule base, not on image interpretation.
A. CONFIGURATION

The layer calls the Gemini API [57] (generateContent endpoint) with the model set by the environment variable GEMINI_MODEL, temperature 0.2, and JSON output mode (responseMimeType = application/json), sending one image (JPEG, PNG, WebP, or GIF, at most ≈9 MB) per request; an OpenAI-compatible endpoint can be configured instead. The evaluation of Section VIII-F used the Gemini endpoint with gemini-3.5-flash-lite, one request per panel, run on November 9, 2026, with the frozen configuration in Supplementary Material S4; the pixel dimensions of every panel are listed in the panel manifest (S5).
B. PROMPT DESIGN

The system prompt defines the role (“vision observer, not a taxonomic authority”) and ten hard rules, among them: observe first and identify only tentatively; never invent a character; use NOT_OBSERVABLE for characters not clearly visible and UNCERTAIN for visible but ambiguous ones; never mark ABSENT unless the region is exposed; keep serial arrangement (CHR_05) and coiling (CHR_06) separate; prefer genus or morphogroup to species; and reply with valid JSON only. It then lists the controlled states of Table II for each character and prescribes the output schema, abridged below (full prompt in Supplementary Material S4).
C. VALIDATION BEFORE SCORING

The VLM response is validated before it reaches the engine: (i) a response without a valid JSON object is rejected; (ii) every character missing from the response is set to NOT_OBSERVABLE; (iii) every state outside {PRESENT, ABSENT, NOT_OBSERVABLE, UNCERTAIN}, every value outside the controlled states of the character, and every PRESENT or ABSENT state without a value are replaced by NOT_OBSERVABLE and logged; (iv) the free-text suggestion (vlm_suggestion) is displayed but never passed to the engine, and the module proposed by the VLM is ignored, the module being derived from CHR_01 as for manual input; and (v) the user reviews and may edit every draft value before scoring.

C. ROBUSTNESS TO INCOMPLETE OBSERVATION: COMPARISON WITH A MULTI-ACCESS KEY

Baseline: Classical multi-access keys of the DELTA/Intkey family [35]–[38] discard every taxon whose coded state differs from an entered observation. The comparator B1 implements this logic on the same knowledge base: every observed mismatch of a mandatory or diagnostic rule eliminates the genus, supporting and contradictory rules are not used, and all surviving genera are tied, so that no ordering advantage is introduced. Both B1 and the proposed engine (A0) take the module from CHR_01, so the 25 genera of the module compete in every case.

E. WEIGHT AND THRESHOLD SENSITIVITY

The weights and thresholds of Section VI were fixed a priori, so their influence was examined around the default A0, w = (wM, wD, wS, wC) = (+3, +5, +1, −5) with τobs = 2, τNM = 3, and δ = 1 (Table XV): unit weights (S1); a reversed hierarchy in which mandatory evidence outweighs diagnostic evidence (S2); no supporting evidence (S3); weak and strong contradiction penalties (S4a, S4b); and the full threshold grid τobs ∈ {1, 2, 3}, τNM ∈ {2, 3, 4}, and δ ∈ {1, 2, 3} with default weights (S5, 27 settings). Each of the 33 configurations was applied to the 104 decision paths and the 150 drafted sheets, and its ranking was compared with that of A0 by RBO and by the share of unchanged top-1 genera (Section VIII-A).

The rankings were stable (Table XV): no weight variant reduced the path RBO below 0.93 or changed Acc@1 by more than 2.4 points. The reversed hierarchy (S2) changed the top-1 genus most often and raised Acc@3 at the expense of Acc@1, whereas S1 and S2 issued far fewer CONFIRMED_GENUS outputs with a higher share of correct ones, i.e., a more conservative but less informative engine. The thresholds do not alter scores and leave every ranking unchanged (RBO = 1 for all 27 settings); they act only on the confidence states: τNM had no effect because no path reached NO_MATCH_WITHIN_CORE_TAXA, δ = 2 and δ = 3 reduced the CONFIRMED_GENUS outputs from 29 to 25 and 14, and τobs = 3 reduced the coverage from 85.6% to 75.0% and Acc@1 to 21.3%. On the drafted sheets, Acc@1 stayed between 3.2% and 3.6% under every setting. No setting dominated the default, which was therefore retained; selecting weights on these development data would overfit them.
F. ZERO-SHOT VISION-LANGUAGE MODEL STRESS TEST

Panel: The stress test uses 150 published image panels of 24 core genera of the ontology: 33 agglutinated, 37 porcelaneous, and 80 hyaline panels from 30 source/section clusters (Table XVI). Twenty-eight panels came from two additional articles (23 Coskinolina panels from [58] and five Alveolina panels from [59]) and 122 from BouDagher-Fadel [2], a book that is also a knowledge-base reference (Section IV-A), so the two cohorts are reported separately. The unit of analysis is an image panel, not a verified independent specimen: panels from the same plate or section can be correlated, and some crops include parts of adjacent sections of the same genus. All sources are published under CC BY 4.0; the panels are reproduced with attribution and a statement of modification in Supplementary Material S5.

Model run: The setting is deliberately zero-shot: a general-purpose model without fine-tuning, exemplars, or calibration. Panel identities and crop coordinates were frozen before the run; taxon-name labels were cropped from the panels of [59], while structural annotations and scale bars within the crops remain and may provide cues; no image was synthesized or enhanced. One pass of gemini-3.5-flash-lite (temperature 0.2) was run per panel (IMG_001–IMG_150) with the prompt and normalization routine of the application, without reference labels, file names, or module assignments. The archived sheets were scored offline by the repaired engine, with the module derived from the drafted CHR_01 and without review or correction. The confidence states were not calibrated on unreviewed drafts (Fig. 7). The ordering Prec(CONFIRMED) > Prec(CANDIDATE) expected of a calibrated engine was thus reversed: confidently wrong drafted states meet the separation condition (5) with spurious diagnostic evidence, so CONFIRMED_GENUS cannot indicate correctness for unreviewed model input (on the decision paths, 17 of 29 identified the leaf genus; Table XII).

Interpretation: The stress test isolates the failure mode that motivates the architecture: randomly masked or corrupted rule-consistent inputs degrade the engine gracefully (Sections VIII-C to VIII-E), whereas systematic misreadings of thin-section morphology by an uncalibrated zero-shot model drive the same engine to wrong exclusions and spurious confirmations. Separating misreadings from rule-card errors requires the planned review with expert-approved character sheets (Section VIII-G). General-purpose vision-language models can therefore serve at most as drafting assistants whose output a specialist reviews, while the taxonomic decision rests on the expert-supervised, deterministic ontology layer, in line with the evidence on fine-grained traits [41], [42].
G. PLANNED BLINDED EXPERT REVIEW OF LLM-DRAFTED OBSERVATIONS

Design: The expert-input evaluation is designed as blinded expert review of LLM-drafted observations, not as unaided expert character extraction. For each case, gemini-3.5-flash-lite [57] (temperature 0.2) receives only the coded views and the frozen 21-character vocabulary, with a morphology-only prompt that requests no genus; no reference genus, publication identity, earlier prediction, rule card, or A0/B1 result is supplied. It returns controlled values, observation states, and short visual reasons, kept with the raw provider response as an immutable LLM_DRAFT record with model version, prompt digest, image checksums, and timestamps. CHR_21 records orientation and is not scored, and, unlike the normalization of Section VII-C, NOT_OBSERVABLE and UNCERTAIN are never promoted automatically. Two reviewers not involved in rule development (EXP01, EXP02) will review the same raw draft independently, approving, correcting, or neutralizing every character and documenting each correction; the draft, each final sheet, and the change trail remain separate, and only a completed form approved by its reviewer (EXPERT_VERIFIED) can enter the comparison. Reference labels, the other reviewer’s changes, and algorithm outputs are withheld during review, and a separate expert (REF01) will verify the reference genera from collection documentation and specimen examination. Because a shared draft can anchor both reviewers, the design does not measure unaided expert performance, and two fixed reviewers do not represent the wider specialist population.

Preparation status: P001–P010 are ten previously evaluated published image panels prepared for a form-usability exercise, taken from the 150 panels of Section VIII-F as archived in the historical V27 evaluation package; they are not independent specimens, and the pilot tests only drafting, form use, review time, and correction recording. One successful generation per case, without selection, yielded 10 LLM_DRAFT records with 210 character entries; the configured gemini-3.6-flash returned HTTP 503 twice before any draft existed, so gemini-3.5-flash-lite was used for availability, and the failed attempts are retained. The drafts assign 133 PRESENT, 41 ABSENT, 23 NOT_OBSERVABLE, and 13 UNCERTAIN states; these are unverified model outputs, not estimates of observation correctness. Twenty review forms (two per case) await completion; no expert-approved form, REF01 verification, or assignment of persons to the role codes exists yet, and F001–F060 remain unassigned. Software tests on synthetic fixtures and a browser test of the review form passed as technical checks, and the analysis gate rejects the incomplete study.

Planned confirmatory study: After the pilot review and the protocol lock, the planning target, not the result of a power calculation, is 60 new documented Paleocene–Eocene fossils of the three wall-composition modules, unused in rule development and in the earlier evaluation; multiple views of a fossil remain one specimen, and pilot images are excluded. The two approved sheets of each fossil will be passed unchanged to the frozen V29 A0 engine and the eliminative comparator B1 (Section VIII-C), identified by the checksums of their four files (S10) and distinct from the V27 package; the CHR_01 entry of each sheet, not the reference module, routes the case, and references are joined only after scoring. The primary estimand is the paired A0 − B1 difference in tie-fractional top-1 agreement (6), averaging the two reviewers’ credits within each fossil and then across fossils; its 95% percentile interval will come from 5000 paired cluster-bootstrap resamples (seed 20261112) that keep the fossils of one source cluster, both reviewers, and both methods together. Secondary endpoints are top-3 agreement, coverage, rule-based reference exclusion, and module-based reference omission. The 120 forms count as 60 specimens, and no result table will be reported before new material, both approved forms, and verified references are available.
DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS

Scope: The ontology covers 75 Paleocene–Eocene genera; Mesozoic or Miocene assemblages will require new rule cards and possibly new character identifiers. First candidates for addition are the unencoded Turkish genera of Section I (Karsella, Orduina, Malatyna, Vania, Haymanella, Kayseriella, Elazigella, Orduella), the missing Tethyan Eocene genera named in Section IV, and the Paleogene cyclamminids.

Closed-world assumption: An unencoded genus is either excluded everywhere (NO_MATCH_WITHIN_CORE_TAXA) or assigned to the closest encoded genus (Section VII-D); graded states mitigate but do not remove this risk. Planned extensions are a display of the module’s genus list with every result and an “out-of-scope” check against genera recorded in the literature but not encoded.

Section orientation (CHR_21): An oblique section can be mislabeled by the user or by the VLM (e.g., as GLOBULAR), so the specialist remains the final arbiter. Early nummulitid genera such as Nummulitoides may not be identifiable from one section, because involution (CHR_08) and marginal-cord thickness (CHR_17) must be judged together from axial and equatorial information; until sections of one specimen can be combined, such cases remain PROBABLE or CANDIDATE. Using CHR_21 to flag orientation-sensitive characters is planned.

Knowledge-base maintenance: Rule cards, trees, and mappings are kept in versioned JSON master files from which the OWL file and the graph are regenerated; each release is to receive a semantic version, an archived DOI, and a change log. The audit, repair scripts, consistency test (api/test/consistency.test.js, eval/consistency_and_audit.py), and ontology validator are rerun before every release; running them as continuous integration and recording the release in each identification report are planned.

Taxonomic revision and synonymy: Genus concepts change through revision and synonymization under the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature [61]. The WoRMS check, run on the stored AphiaID, flags names that are no longer accepted and gives the accepted name. After a synonymy, the junior name becomes an alias of the senior genus node, the curator merges or revises the rule cards, and the release notes record the change; genera are never renamed automatically. A live WoRMS lookup (Supplementary Material S1) returned records for 42 of the 75 names and none for 33; a missing record does not invalidate a fossil genus name, but these 33 names, the record returned for Idalina (a molluscan junior homonym), and Planocamerinoides (returned as unaccepted) require curator verification.

User bias: Decision-support systems can induce automation bias [62]. The workflow counters it by recording observations before any ranking is shown, showing the supporting and contradicting evidence of every genus, and avoiding a single forced answer; the overconfident outputs on unreviewed drafts (Section VIII-F) show why every draft needs specialist review. Recording the sheet first limits, but cannot remove, the influence of the expert’s expectations, because a specialist may recognize a genus while describing it; a shared model draft can likewise anchor the reviewers of Section VIII-G.

Prompt and image quality in the VLM layer: Even with a consistent prompt, image resolution, optics, and preservation affect the VLM output; thin-section fine-tuning or a segmentation model (e.g., YOLO-based [63]) is planned.

Threats to validity: (i) The rule cards were extended from seven pilot taxa to 75 genera by single-author literature synthesis; the audit secures internal consistency, not taxonomic correctness, and 28 genera still lack a scoring diagnostic rule (Section IV-B). (ii) Decision paths and synthetic profiles derive from the knowledge base itself, so Tables XII–XV characterize inference on rule-consistent inputs, not accuracy on independent specimens. (iii) The 150 panels of Section VIII-F are correlated published images, 122 from a knowledge-base reference, that the model may have seen in training. (iv) The published reference genus may itself be disputed. Points (ii)–(iv) motivate the study planned in Section VIII-G, not yet conducted; point (i) is addressed in Section X.

Genus level only: All rule cards are defined at genus level. Species discrimination in larger benthic foraminifera often relies on numerical parameters (number of whorls, chamber expansion rate, embryonic-apparatus size, diameter/thickness ratio), which will require measured values and interval criteria in the character model.
CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This study presented a transparent and extensible genus identification ontology for Paleocene–Eocene benthic foraminifera and a decision-support model built on it, whose deterministic, evidence-weighted inference over 21 controlled characters and 706 graded rule cards for 75 genera is traceable to morphological statements and is published as an OWL 2 ontology verified by HermiT. After a logged audit-driven repair, the engine ranks the leaf genus first on 53 of 104 decision paths, and 17 of its 29 CONFIRMED_GENUS outputs are correct (14 of 48 before). Graded evidence outperformed an eliminative multi-access key at every level of missingness, the rankings were stable under alternative weightings, and treating unobservable characters as absent was the most damaging design alternative. Unreviewed zero-shot vision-language-model drafts drove the engine to wrong exclusions and spurious confirmations, supporting the confinement of such models to drafting observations for expert review.

The system is a working end-to-end prototype that supports, rather than replaces, the specialist. Future priorities are: (i) the blinded expert review of LLM-drafted observations planned in Section VIII-G, followed by a comparison of drafted character values with expert sheets and an open-set, multi-institutional evaluation with and without the system; (ii) per-rule bibliographic provenance, vocabulary extensions for the 28 genera without a scoring diagnostic rule, correction of the tree–rule conflicts of Section VIII-B, and community review of the rule cards; (iii) the Turkish genera of Section I and Paleogene cyclamminids such as Cyclammina; (iv) an image layer fine-tuned on thin sections or supported by segmentation [63]; (v) other intervals; and (vi) multi-section analysis of differently oriented sections of one specimen, critical for separating nummulitid genera.
